articles.title: Sheriffs Who Supported Trump's Immigration Enforcement Efforts Voted Out
articles.summary: A significant number of sheriffs who supported President Donald Trump's immigration enforcement efforts have been voted out of office by their constituents.
articles.content: In a significant shift, some sheriffs who supported President Donald Trump's immigration enforcement efforts have been voted out of office by their constituents. A striking example is Alamance County in North Carolina, where Shannon Long ran against incumbent Republican Sheriff Terry Johnson. Long, a pastor and former sheriff's deputy, faced challenges winning over voters due to the strained relationship between law enforcement and the county's growing Latino community. Long's campaign encountered difficulties when potential supporters would not speak with him, allegedly because they felt intimidated by the presence of his campaign van displaying the title "sheriff. This sentiment reflects a deeper issue - many Latino residents in Alamance County feel marginalized, oppressed and depressed due to their experiences with immigration enforcement. According to Long, who defeated Johnson after the election, these voters often express feelings of not belonging in their community. He attributed this atmosphere of fear to the policies implemented by Johnson's office in cooperation with the Trump administration. The ousting of Johnson and a few other sheriffs is seen as a potential warning sign for those who have collaborated with President Donald Trump's mass deportation efforts. While it may be too early to determine the full impact, these results could hinder agreements that are crucial to the administration's immigration enforcement strategy. Local law enforcement cooperation with federal immigration authorities has been a contentious issue on the campaign trail in several states this year. In Indiana, voters ousted a sheriff who had signed a 287(g) agreement allowing his deputies to enforce federal immigration laws. The agreements have become a significant factor in some elections, particularly in regions where they are most prevalent. The South is home to the majority of these cooperative pacts, which deputize local law officers and contribute significantly to ICE's arrest numbers. Government data shows that over 29,000 local law enforcement officials have been deputized under these agreements, resulting in thousands of arrests each month. In July alone, more than 6,600 arrests were made by these deputies, accounting for about 15% of all ICE arrests. Many sheriffs whose offices had signed 287(g) agreements faced opposition from candidates who campaigned on a promise to curtail cooperation with federal immigration authorities. The issue is likely to resurface in two years when several states with large numbers of these agreements hold elections. Alamance County, a traditionally Republican stronghold in North Carolina, has undergone significant demographic changes over the years. The county's population has grown increasingly diverse, with a notable shift from a small Hispanic community of 750 residents in 1990 to nearly 25,000 in 2020. Sheriff Terry Johnson, who was first elected in 2002 and has been a polarizing figure, insisted that his office welcomes lawful immigrants. However, allegations of racial profiling against minority residents have persisted, including a Justice Department lawsuit over a decade ago that ended with a settlement. The county's reputation as a place where minority groups feel marginalized and excluded from the political process is reflected in its nickname No Chance Alamance." According to school board member Seneca Rogers, this perception stems from a sense of unjust policing and lack of representation among Black and Latino residents. Sheriff Johnson initially attributed his loss to immigration policy, but later clarified that it was unlikely a major factor. Instead, he pointed to the long-term effects of his tenure in office and the national political environment, which proved particularly challenging for Republicans in North Carolina during the last election cycle. The ousting of sheriffs who participated in Trump's immigration enforcement efforts has had far-reaching implications for local communities. Many residents were hesitant to interact with law enforcement due to concerns about racial profiling and biased policing practices. Community organizer Leslie Arevalo noted that non-white residents often felt targeted, especially during traffic stops. Voters like Renee Russell welcomed the change in leadership, citing a need for fresh perspectives on community engagement and public safety. The election of the county's first Black sheriff was seen as a positive step towards greater representation and accountability. State Senator Amy Galey defended the outgoing sheriff's record, highlighting improvements to training programs and mental health services. However, she acknowledged that concerns about immigration enforcement tactics may have contributed to broader worries about law enforcement. The shift away from immigration enforcement pacts is also being felt in other parts of the country, including Frederick County, Maryland, where Republican Sheriff Chuck Jenkins previously participated in the 287(g) program. Public sentiment against certain sheriffs who signed pacts to aid Trump's immigration enforcement efforts has been mounting across the country. In Maryland's Frederick County, for instance, Republican Sheriff Chuck Jenkins faced opposition after participating in the 287(g) program. He acknowledged that the program likely cost him his reelection bid but still maintained it made the community safer. However, not everyone shared Jenkins' views on the matter. Retired social worker Carol Antoniewicz, a vocal supporter of Democrat Karl Bickel, who defeated Jenkins in the election, said that people are fed up with negative attitudes towards immigrants. She distributed campaign literature and emails to promote Bickel's candidacy, which focused on his pledge not to cooperate with ICE. The immigration debate also played out in Wisconsin's Winnebago County, where a schoolteacher's arrest by ICE sparked widespread outrage just before the election. This backlash had far-reaching implications for local politics, making any perceived alignment with immigration officers a liability for candidates. Local advocate and immigration lawyer Molly Smiltneek noted that this perception has become a major concern in recent elections. The sheriff's department in Winnebago County was not directly involved in the teacher's arrest but its 287(g) agreement became a central issue in the election campaign. Democrat Jason Rippl, who won the election, promised to end the program, which resonated with voters seeking change on immigration issues. Rippl's victory marked another instance of public sentiment shifting against sheriffs who had signed pacts to aid Trump's immigration enforcement efforts. As newly elected officials take office, they are being asked to reconsider their stances on immigration-related programs like 287(g). In some cases, this means re-evaluating agreements made with ICE. The shift away from these partnerships is a significant development in the ongoing debate over immigration policy and law enforcement priorities. The shift away from partnerships between law enforcement agencies and the Trump administration's immigration enforcement efforts has significant implications for the communities affected by these policies. In response to this shift, some local sheriffs are seeking to rebuild trust with immigrant communities. To achieve this goal, a sheriff has been holding meetings with community leaders in an effort to establish new relationships and foster cooperation between law enforcement and Latino residents. The aim is to create a sense of security and inclusivity, where people feel empowered to engage with the authorities without fear of repercussions. By doing so, he hopes to demonstrate that the sheriff's office is committed to serving all members of the community. articles.title: Protests against rising cost of living continue across France
articles.summary: The number of protesters nationwide decreased from 200,000 last week to an estimated 150,000 this Saturday, according to organisers.
articles.content: Protests against the rising cost of living continued across France for the sixth consecutive Saturday, but saw a significant decrease in turnout compared to previous weeks. According to organisers, 150,000 people participated in nationwide protests, down from last week's figure of 200,000. The interior ministry reported a substantially lower number, putting the overall count at 82,500 protesters across the country. This represents a decline from the 106,000 recorded last Saturday. The discrepancy between the figures highlights the ongoing debate over the true extent of public involvement in these demonstrations. Cities across France witnessed tens of thousands of people taking to the streets, with one notable gathering occurring in central Paris's Place de la République square. A festive atmosphere prevailed as musicians played, food trucks sold their wares, and protesters donned costumes and held homemade signs. The protest movement, which began in mid-September when high school students demanded improved learning conditions, has since grown into a broader campaign against rising prices and inadequate public services. The issue of police brutality has also become a focal point for demonstrators. The diversity of protesters was evident in their flags and vests, which blended together trade union symbols, left-wing party emblems, student organisation logos, and Yellow Vest movement insignia. This eclectic mix marked a significant milestone for the Yellow Vests, now eight years past their initial protests that shook President Emmanuel Macron's government. In a poignant gesture, one group set up mock headstones to commemorate the demise of France's public services, including social security and education systems. The stark reminder of the state of these essential services was a powerful message, underscoring the struggles faced by citizens across various sectors. Manon Moret, general secretary of the students' union Unef, pointed out that young people in multiple countries are grappling with similar issues: precarity has become a widespread concern, forcing individuals to choose between basic needs like housing, healthcare, and food. This stark reality was evident in the placards held by protesters. Placards carried messages such as "I want to live, not survive" and "No to the licence to kill", referencing a recently adopted law that has been heavily criticised for increasing protection for law enforcement officers who use their weapons. The protests have been largely peaceful but have seen instances of fringe violence and accusations of police brutality. At least 31 people have suffered serious injuries at the hands of security forces since the protests began, according to an AFP count based on direct testimonies, victims' lawyers, and NGO records. Despite these incidents, authorities have yet to provide a comprehensive toll of injuries. The protests against the police law in France continued for a sixth consecutive Saturday, but this time around, the turnout was significantly lower than in previous weeks. Some cities reported smaller numbers of demonstrators taking to the streets, despite calls from unions and activists for more protests in the coming weeks. In Lille, Marseille, and Lyon, protesters marched peacefully, carrying signs and banners. However, not all demonstrations remained calm, as some individuals attempted to rally in areas that had been banned. Clashes broke out on the fringes of a few protests, with riot police facing off against demonstrators who set fire to vehicles and bins. Police responded by firing tear gas at the crowds, but overall, the situation was less intense than in previous weeks. Authorities had taken precautions ahead of time, anticipating potential troublemakers among the protesters. Despite some incidents of violence, many participants remained committed to their cause, with some expressing optimism that their efforts would eventually lead to positive change. As one protester noted, "If we take care of our young people, our students, we'll have a wonderful tomorrow and that's why I'm here." With more protests planned for the coming weeks, it remains to be seen whether the momentum will continue or begin to fade. articles.title: Unprecedented Material Properties Observed in Polymer Under Stress
articles.summary: A team led by Chenfeng Ke has made a breakthrough discovery about the behavior of materials under stress, developing a smart material that exhibits unprecedented properties such as memory and adaptability.
articles.content: A team led by Chenfeng Ke has made an unusual discovery about the behavior of materials under stress. While most substances tend to weaken over time, this group's innovative polymer appears to grow stronger with repeated bending and straining. According to Ke, their smart material exhibits properties that are unprecedented in the field: it can remember, adapt, learn, and even grow. The implications of such a discovery are vast and exciting, as researchers consider potential applications for this remarkable substance. The breakthrough was achieved through a combination of sugar crystals and polyethylene glycol, a compound commonly used in laxatives and other health products. This biodegradable blend forms a hydrogel, which is a flexible material capable of absorbing and retaining large amounts of water. The hydrogel exhibits remarkable properties when subjected to repeated bending. Instead of deteriorating, its strength and resilience increase. This phenomenon was observed during experiments where the material was flexed numerous times, a process that could potentially be mimicked in various real-world applications. At the heart of this hydrogel's exceptional performance lies cyclodextrin, a sugar-based compound with unique properties. When the polymer is stretched or bent, the cyclodextrin molecules slide into position to reinforce areas under strain, effectively adapting to the changing conditions. This dynamic response allows the material to maintain its integrity even in the face of repeated deformation. The hydrogel's ability to mimic biological materials has significant implications for medical applications. By emulating the properties of collagen, a protein found in skin and other connective tissues, this polymer could potentially be used to protect and repair damaged tissues. This approach draws inspiration from nature, where many remarkable smart materials can be found. Surgeons and orthopedic device manufacturers may find this material particularly appealing due to its biocompatibility with biological tissues. Its composition of sugar and polyethylene glycol makes it an attractive option for medical applications. The potential uses for this sugar-based hydrogel are numerous and varied, with applications in medical fields such as supporting artificial joints or repairing damaged tissues. In both cases, areas that don't experience stress or strain would remain soft and pliable, allowing the material to adapt to different situations. According to Ke, a chemist who has been working on this project, the material doesn't need to be rigid to function effectively in the body. "If you're putting material into a body, you don't necessarily want it to be completely rigid," he explained, emphasizing the importance of flexibility and adaptability. Ke acknowledges that his expertise lies in chemistry rather than medicine or medical device development, which is why he's eager to collaborate with experts from WashU Medicine and other institutions. We want to work with these specialists to explore the possibilities of this material, he said, hoping that their research will attract interest from investors and potential users. The team has so far produced small quantities of the new polymer, in tens of grams at a time, but they're confident that production can be scaled up once the concept is proven. With successful demonstrations under their belt, Ke and his team are now exploring ways to expand their research and make the material more widely available. The research team has successfully demonstrated that their sugar-based hydrogel material can be strengthened through repeated bending, rather than being worn down by it. This counterintuitive property suggests a range of potential applications for the material, which could be used to create self-healing structures or adaptive systems that respond to changing conditions.
